claims.text: Localized friction stir processing avoids melting and solidification in the repaired region.
Avoiding melting and solidification mitigates solidification-induced hot cracking.
Friction stir processing refines the material microstructure.
Friction stir processing can restore or enhance mechanical performance relative to fusion-weld repair.
The component material is highly susceptible to hot cracking during fusion-welding thermal cycles.
Incorporating HEA particles during FSP and applying subsequent heat treatment can produce a graded, dual-layered core-shell interface.
The repaired component will operate under high thermal gradients and cyclic mechanical loads characteristic of severe aerospace or high-performance service.
A refined, compositionally graded dual-layer interface reduces residual stresses.
A refined, compositionally graded dual-layer interface blocks crack initiation.
FSP produces severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization.
Controlled post-FSP heat treatment produces a gradual compositional and microstructural transition at an HEA-particle/aluminum interface.
The heat-treatment-induced interfacial transition enhances bonding and toughness.
The FSP-repaired region will have greater tensile strength and ductility than a conventional fusion-welded repair.
The FSP-repaired region will have a significantly lower hot-cracking propensity than a conventional fusion-welded repair.
FSP repair will extend service life under aggressive operating conditions.
Traditional fusion-welding repair typically produces hot cracking because of rapid solidification and high thermal stresses.
Traditional fusion-welding repair produces inferior mechanical properties.
The repair remains effective when operating temperatures stay below the FSP tool limits.
The scalability of FSP repair to complex geometries and varied damage profiles is uncertain.
It is uncertain whether HEA particles consistently improve interfacial bonding across different material systems.
